progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From v01: eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; the shared kit (membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA); mitochondria release energy from glucose (one example in v01 scene 5). From Stage 5 (assumed, not re-taught): cells carry out respiration to release energy (word equation level); plants make glucose by photosynthesis using light; DNA carries inherited information. Not assumed: phospholipid, partially permeable, cellulose, nuclear envelope, nuclear pore, amino acid, protein synthesis, endoplasmic reticulum, rough and smooth ER, lipid, Golgi body, vesicle, cristae, ATP, aerobic respiration, lysosome, digestive enzyme, vacuole, turgor, chloroplast, chlorophyll.
progression.startsWith: Here's the eukaryotic cell from last time, the one with its DNA inside a nucleus. It's crowded with organelles, and some of them hold enzymes strong enough to digest the cell itself. So why doesn't it? And how does a cell build a protein and send it out? Let's meet the eleven structures you need, grouped by job, and follow one protein out of the cell.
progression.stopsAfter: describing, for each of the eleven structures, one structural feature and its function (cell membrane, cytoplasm, cell wall, nucleus, ribosomes, rough and smooth ER, Golgi body, mitochondria, lysosomes, vacuoles, chloroplasts); tracing a protein from instructions in the nucleus to a ribosome on the rough ER, folding in the ER, a vesicle to the Golgi body, packaging, a vesicle to the cell membrane and release; explaining that mitochondria transfer energy from glucose to ATP rather than making energy; explaining that the lysosome's membrane keeps its digestive enzymes away from the rest of the cell; predicting well-developed organelles from a cell's job; predicting the effect of a block in the production line.
progression.nextLesson: why plant and animal cells differ (route entry bio-y11-fa1-v03).

teaching.task: *What does each eukaryotic organelle do, and how do they work together to make and export a protein?*
teaching.causalExplanation: Start at the edge. The cell membrane is a very thin double layer of fatty molecules called phospholipids, with proteins set into it. It's partially permeable, which means it lets some substances through and blocks others, so it controls what enters and leaves. Inside is the cytoplasm, a jelly-like fluid where many reactions happen and the organelles sit. Plant cells add a cell wall outside the membrane. It's made of cellulose, a tough fibre, and it's rigid, so it gives the cell its shape and support. Animal cells don't have one. The nucleus is usually the largest organelle. It's wrapped in two membranes, called the nuclear envelope, which are dotted with pores. Inside is the cell's DNA. The nucleus controls the cell, because that DNA carries the instructions for every protein the cell makes. Copies of those instructions leave through the pores, heading to where proteins are built. They go to the ribosomes. These are tiny, made of two parts, with no membrane around them. Some float free in the cytoplasm, and many sit on a membrane network beside the nucleus. A ribosome reads the copied instructions and joins building blocks called amino acids into a chain, and that chain becomes a protein. So ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis, which just means making proteins.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Here's the eukaryotic cell from last time, the one with its DNA inside a nucleus. Start at the edge. The nucleus is usually the largest organelle. They go to the ribosomes.
teaching.openingDecision: opens on v01's handoff frame: m5x-cell-protein-synthesis-v1.png alone at the centre at about 60 per cent of frame height, the "Next" chip at the lower right, the camera mid-push towards the nucleus. The chip lifts and becomes the heading: "How do eukaryotic organelles work together?" On "its DNA inside a nucleus" the nucleus outline traces once (v01's cue, recalled). On "crowded with organelles" the camera pulls back slightly and the rough ER, Golgi stack and mitochondria pulse in turn, unlabelled. On "enzymes strong enough to digest the cell itself" a scribbleEllipse circles two of the small pink spheres and a grey "?" tag sits beside them (named in scene 9). On "build a protein and send it out" a short coded dashed path draws from the nucleus, past the ER and Golgi stack, to the membrane, then fades. On "eleven structures" the coded organelle tracker draws at the right edge, eleven names in three colour bands: "cell membrane, cytoplasm, cell wall, nucleus" (boundary and control); "ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi body" (production line); "mitochondria, lysosomes, vacuoles, chloroplasts" (energy, digestion, storage). At most three bright items besides the tracker. Hold half a second.
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. Cells in the pancreas make large amounts of a digestive enzyme, which is a protein, and release it from the cell. Predict three organelles that would be unusually well developed in these cells, and justify each choice by its function. Pause here to answer. Second. A drug stops vesicles from leaving the Golgi body. A cell treated with the drug normally makes a protein and exports it. Predict where the protein will build up in the cell, and explain what happens to its export. Pause here to answer.
